metric.why: Liquid-cooled AI racks with coolant, manifolds, and batteries are dramatically heavier than the enterprise racks most buildings were engineered for. Retrofit projects hit structural limits before electrical ones more often than the industry expected.
metric.definition: The structural weight the raised floor or slab supports per square foot, against the actual weight of installed racks.

reading.body:
Liquid-cooled AI racks weigh more than the floors in most existing data centers can support, making structural limits a binding constraint on retrofit projects before power delivery becomes one.

Enterprise data centers were engineered for server densities built around air-cooled equipment. Liquid cooling systems add weight through coolant, manifolds, and batteries. The raised floors and concrete slabs in these buildings have structural ratings measured in pounds per square foot, set decades ago for lighter loads. When operators try to pack dense AI racks into existing space, they hit the building's weight capacity before they exhaust the electrical infrastructure.

This inverts the typical retrofit sequence. Most data center upgrades run into power limits first: how much power the facility can deliver, and how much cooling capacity exists to reject that heat. Here, the floor itself becomes the wall. A retrofit project discovers it cannot add more racks to a given section without structural reinforcement, which means foundation work, which means downtime and capital that was budgeted for electrical or cooling upgrades instead.

The metric does not reveal how often this happens across the installed base, or which regions and building vintages are most affected. It does not cover new construction, where floors can be engineered for higher loads from the start. But it highlights why compute scaling depends not just on power and cooling available, but on the physical plant that was built to house older, lighter equipment.
